subsection: 5. Eggs: structure, nutritional significance and contribution to the diet

notes.b: The outside of the egg is built to protect the liquid contents while still letting the egg breathe. The air cell inside it is a useful clue to how old the egg is.
points: Shell: hard and porous, made mainly of calcium carbonate. It protects the contents, and the tiny pores let gases pass in and out.
The outer coating of the shell (the cuticle, or bloom) reduces the entry of bacteria.
Shell colour, white or brown, depends on the breed of hen, so it does not affect the nutritive value.
Shell membranes: two thin membranes, an outer and an inner one, line the shell and help keep bacteria out.

Air cell (air space): a pocket between the two membranes at the blunt, broad end of the egg. It grows as the egg ages because water evaporates through the shell, so a bigger air cell means an older egg.
Water test for freshness: a fresh egg sinks and lies flat in water because its air cell is small, while an old egg floats because its air cell is large.
Diagram: a cross-section of an egg, labelling the shell, shell membranes and air cell.
notes.tip: The air cell is at the blunt end, not the pointed end. Shell colour is not a measure of quality or nutrition, so do not use it as a point about nutritive value.

notes.h: Albumen, chalazae, yolk and germinal disc
notes.b: Inside the shell are two liquid parts, the white and the yolk. Cords and membranes hold the yolk in the centre so it is cushioned from knocks.
points: Albumen (white): the transparent liquid around the yolk. It is mainly water (about 90%) and protein (albumin, ovalbumin and globulin), and it is fat free.
The albumen has two layers, thick and thin. The thick white is the sign of a fresh egg.
Chalazae: two twisted cords of albumen at each end of the yolk that anchor the yolk in the centre of the egg. They are not the same thing as the germinal disc.
Yolk: the yellow centre, held in the vitelline membrane. It holds the fat, lecithin, cholesterol, protein (vitellin and livetin), the fat-soluble vitamins and minerals, including iron.
Yolk colour depends on the hen's feed, because of carotenoid pigments (yellow-orange colouring) in it.

Germinal disc (blastodisc): a small pale spot on the surface of the yolk. It would develop into a chick if the egg were fertilised, but eggs sold in shops are normally unfertilised. It is not a blood spot or an embryo.
Diagram: a labelled cross-section of the egg showing the shell, outer and inner shell membranes, air cell, thick and thin albumen, chalazae, vitelline membrane, yolk and germinal disc.
notes.tip: You may be asked to draw and label the egg, and to say what the chalazae and the air cell do. The chalazae anchor the yolk, and the air cell shows the age of the egg.

notes.b: An egg packs protein, fat, vitamins and minerals into a small package, but it is missing carbohydrate, fibre and vitamin C. For each nutrient, learn what the egg supplies and what the body uses it for.
points: Protein is about 13% of the egg. It is high biological value (HBV) with a biological value of 100%, because it contains all the essential amino acids in the proportions the body needs. It is used for growth and repair and for making hormones and enzymes.
White protein is albumin (ovalbumin) and globulin. Yolk protein is vitellin and livetin.
Fat is about 12%, all in the yolk. It is mostly saturated and is in a very fine emulsion because of lecithin (a natural emulsifier in the yolk), so it is easily digested. It gives heat and energy.
The white is fat free, and cholesterol is found only in the yolk. The yolk supplies most of the energy of the egg.
Eggs contain no carbohydrate (0%) and no fibre, so they are served with carbohydrate foods such as toast or potatoes, and with fibre.
Fat-soluble vitamins A, D, E and K are found in the yolk. A keeps membranes and eyes healthy, D builds bones and teeth, E is an antioxidant and K helps blood clot.

B group vitamins are found in both the white and the yolk. B1 and B2 help release energy, and niacin and B12 are needed for metabolism. Free-range eggs can contain higher levels of some vitamins, such as niacin and B12, than eggs from caged hens. Eggs lack vitamin C.

Minerals make up about 1% of the egg: calcium and phosphorus for bones and teeth, iron in the yolk for making haemoglobin, and zinc and sulphur. The egg is about 75% water, and the white is mostly water.
notes.tip: For a nutritive value answer, give four to six points and attach a function to each, for example protein for growth and repair. Biological value of 100% is a reference figure, so never say an egg is 100% protein. Say 'no vitamin C, no carbohydrate, no fibre' when asked what is missing.

notes.h: Contribution of eggs to the diet
notes.b: Eggs earn their place in the diet because they are cheap, nutritious, easy to digest and easy to cook. Their weak points, saturated fat and cholesterol and the missing nutrients, are dealt with by moderation and by what they are served with.
points: Eggs are cheap and nutritious, so they suit people on a low budget. They are a protein alternative to meat and fish.
Eggs supply HBV protein for ovo-lacto vegetarians, who eat dairy products and eggs but not meat or fish.
Eggs are easily digested, because the fat is already emulsified and the protein is soft when lightly cooked. This makes them suitable for children, older people, invalids and convalescents.
Their protein supports growth and repair in children, adolescents and pregnant women.

Eggs are quick and easy to cook, which saves fuel, and are versatile in sweet and savoury dishes. They can be eaten alone, or as a meal with carbohydrate such as egg on toast or an omelette with potatoes.
Eggs contain saturated fat and cholesterol, so people with raised cholesterol or heart disease, or anyone limiting cholesterol, should eat eggs in moderation.
Eggs lack vitamin C and fibre, so serve them with complex carbohydrate, vegetables, fruit and wholegrain foods to balance the diet.
Eggs can carry Salmonella (a food poisoning bacterium), so cook them thoroughly for babies, older people, pregnant women and the ill, and wash hands and utensils after handling raw egg.
notes.tip: For a day's menu, use egg as the protein in one meal, such as scrambled egg on wholemeal toast or quiche with salad, and balance it with fibre and vitamin C foods. In a dietetic answer, say cheap, versatile, easily digested and quick to cook, then add caution about saturated fat and cholesterol.

keyTerms.definition: The white of the egg, a watery mixture of proteins that surrounds the yolk.
The yellow centre of the egg, rich in fat, lecithin, cholesterol, vitamins and minerals.
Two cord-like strands of albumen that anchor the yolk in the centre of the egg.
The pocket at the blunt end of the egg between the shell membranes, which enlarges as the egg ages.
One of the two thin membranes lining the shell, which help keep bacteria out.
The small spot on the yolk surface, which would develop into a chick if fertilised.
The main protein in the egg white, which is high biological value.
A person who eats dairy products but no meat, fish or eggs.

questions.prompt: Name three parts of an egg and give the function of each.
questions.model: Shell: protects the contents and allows gases to pass through. Albumen: supplies HBV protein and cushions the yolk. Yolk: supplies fat, fat-soluble vitamins, iron and lecithin. Chalazae: anchor the yolk in the centre. Air cell: indicates the freshness of the egg, enlarging as it ages. Any three parts with functions give full marks.

questions.prompt: Describe the nutritive value of eggs and explain how eggs contribute to the diet of different groups of people.
questions.model: Nutritive value: about 13% HBV protein with 100% biological value (albumin, ovalbumin and globulin in the white; vitellin and livetin in the yolk); about 12% fat, mostly saturated in the yolk, with lecithin and cholesterol; the white is fat-free; no carbohydrate or fibre; fat-soluble vitamins A, D, E and K in the yolk; B group vitamins in both parts; minerals including calcium, phosphorus, iron and zinc; no vitamin C; about 75% water. Contribution: HBV protein for growth and repair in children and adolescents; easily digested for older people and convalescents; protein for lacto-vegetarians; cheap, quick and versatile for families on low budgets; should be served with carbohydrate and vitamin C foods, and eaten in moderation by people limiting cholesterol.
